title: The Jew believes greater wonders in the prophets
source_text: Φήσομεν οὖν πρῶτον ὅτι, εἰ μὲν ὁ ἀπιστῶν τῷ περὶ τοῦ εἴδους τῆς περιστερᾶς φάσματι τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος ἀνεγέγραπτο Ἐπικούρειος εἶναι ἢ Δημοκρίτειος ἢ Περιπατητικὸς, χώραν ἂν εἶχεν ἀκόλουθον τῷ προσωποποιουμένῳ τὸ λεγόμενον· νυνὶ δὲ οὐδὲ τοῦθ᾿ ὁ σοφώτατος Κέλσος ἑώρακεν, ὅτι Ἰουδαίῳ, πλείονα πιστεύοντι καὶ παραδοξότερα ἐκ τῶν προφητικῶν γραφῶν τῆς περὶ τοῦ εἴδους τῆς περιστερᾶς ἱστορίας, τὸν τοιοῦτον περιέθηκε λόγον. εἴποι γὰρ ἄν τις τῷ Ἰουδαίῳ, περὶ τοῦ φάσματος ἀπιστοῦντι καὶ οἰομένῳ κατηγορεῖν αὐτοῦ ὡς πλάσματος· σὺ δὲ πόθεν, ὦ οὗτος, ἀποδεῖξαι ἂν ἔχοις ὅτι εἶπε κύριος ὁ θεὸς τῷ Ἀδὰμ ἢ τῇ Εὔᾳ ἢ τῷ Κάϊν ἢ τῷ Νῶε ἢ τῷ Ἀβραὰμ ἢ τῷ Ἰσαὰκ ἢ τῷ Ἰακὼβ τὰ ἀναγεγραμμένα αὐτὸν εἰρηκέναι τοῖς ἀνδράσι τούτοις; ἵνα δὲ τῇ ἱστορίᾳ ταύτῃ ἱστορίαν παραβάλω, εἴποιμ᾿ ἂν πρὸς τὸν Ἰουδαῖον· καὶ ὁ σὸς Ἰεζεκιὴλ ἀνέγραψε λέγων· „ἠνοίχθησαν οἱ οὐρανοὶ, καὶ εἶδον ὅρασιν θεοῦ,“ ηντινα διηγησάμενος ἐπιφέρει αὐτῇ· „αὕτη ἡ ὅρασις ὁμοιώματος δόξης κυρίου· καὶ εἶπε πρός με.“ εἰ γὰρ ψευδῆ τὰ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀναγεγραμμένα, ἐπεὶ μὴ ἔχομεν, ὡς ὑπολαμβάνεις, ἐναργῶς παραστῆσαι, πῶς ταῦτά ἐστιν ἀληθῆ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ μόνου ἑωραμένα ἢ ἀκουσθέντα καὶ, ὡς ἔδοξας τετηρηκέναι, καὶ ὑπὸ ἑνὸς τῶν κολασθέντων· τί οὐχὶ μᾶλλον καὶ τὸν Ἰεζεκιὴλ φήσομεν τερατευόμενον εἰρηκέναι τὸ „ἠνοίχθησαν οἱ οὐρανοὶ“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς; ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐὰν ὁ Ἡσαΐας φάσκῃ· „εἶδον τὸν κύριον Σαβαὼθ καθήμενον ἐπὶ θρόνου ὑψηλοῦ καὶ ἐπηρμένου· καὶ τὰ Σεραφὶμ εἱστήκεισαν κύκλῳ αὐτοῦ, ἓξ πτέρυγες τῷ ἑνὶ καὶ ἓξ πτέρυγες τῷ ἑνὶ“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, πόθεν, ὅτι ἀληθῶς ἑώρακε; πεπίστευκας γὰρ, ὦ Ἰουδαῖε, τούτοις ὡς ἀψευδέσι καὶ ὑπὸ θειοτέρου πνεύματος οὐ μόνον ἑωραμένοις τῷ προφήτῃ ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰρημένοις καὶ ἀναγεγραμμένοις. τίνι δὲ καὶ πιστεύειν μᾶλλον ἄξιον, φάσκοντι ἀνεῷχθαι αὐτῷ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καὶ φωνῆς ἀκηκοέναι ἢ ἑωρακέναι „τὸν κύριον Σαβαὼθ καθήμενον ἐπὶ θρόνου ὑψηλοῦ καὶ ἐπηρμένου,“ Ἡσαΐᾳ καὶ Ἰεζεκιὴλ ἢ τῷ Ἰησοῦ; ἐκείνων μὲν γὰρ ἔργον οὐδὲν τηλικοῦτον εὑρίσκεται· τοῦ δὲ Ἰησοῦ τὸ ἀνδραγάθημα οὐ κατὰ τοὺς αὐτοὺς τῆς ἐνσωματώσεως μόνους γέγονε χρόνους. ἀλλὰ καὶ μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο ἡ Ἰησοῦ δύναμίς ἐστιν ἐνεργοῦσα τὴν ἐπιστροφὴν καὶ τὴν βελτίωσιν ἐν τοῖς πιστεύουσι δι᾿ αὐτοῦ τῷ θεῷ. ἐναργὲς δὲ δεῖγμα τοῦ δυνάμει αὐτοῦ ταῦτα γίνεσθαι τὸ, ὡς αὐτός φησι καὶ καταλαμβάνεται, μὴ ὄντων ἐργατῶν τῶν ἐργαζομένων τὸν θερισμὸν τῶν ψυχῶν, τοσοῦτον εἶναι θερισμὸν συγκομιζομένων καὶ συναγομένων εἰς τὰς πανταχοῦ ἅλωνας τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἐκκλησίας.
pass_a_gloss: We shall say first then that, if the one disbelieving (ἀπιστῶν) the apparition (φάσμα) of the Holy Spirit in the form (εἶδος) of the dove had been written up (ἀνεγέγραπτο) as being an Epicurean or Democritean or Peripatetic, what is said would have had a place (χώραν) consistent (ἀκόλουθον) with the character portrayed (προσωποποιουμένῳ); but now not even this has the most wise (σοφώτατος) Celsus seen, that to a Jew, believing more and more marvellous things (παραδοξότερα) from the prophetic Scriptures (προφητικῶν γραφῶν) than the story of the form of the dove, he attached (περιέθηκε) such an argument. For one might say to the Jew, disbelieving about the apparition and thinking to accuse it as a fiction: and you, sir (ὦ οὗτος), from where could you prove (ἀποδεῖξαι) that the Lord God (κύριος ὁ θεός) said to Adam or Eve or Cain or Noah or Abraham or Isaac or Jacob the things recorded that he said to these men? And that I may set beside (παραβάλω) this story a story, I would say to the Jew: your Ezekiel too wrote, saying: The heavens were opened (ἠνοίχθησαν), and I saw a vision (ὅρασιν) of God; which having narrated he adds to it: This [is] the vision of the likeness (ὁμοιώματος) of the glory (δόξης) of the Lord; and he said to me. For if the things written about Jesus are false, since we cannot, as you suppose (ὑπολαμβάνεις), clearly (ἐναργῶς) show (παραστῆσαι) how these are true, seen or heard by him alone, and, as you seemed to have observed (τετηρηκέναι), by one of those punished (κολασθέντων): why shall we not rather say also that Ezekiel, telling marvels (τερατευόμενον), said 'the heavens were opened' and what follows? But also if Isaiah says: I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting on a throne high and lifted up (ἐπηρμένου); and the Seraphim stood around him, six wings to the one and six wings to the one, and what follows, from where [is it known] that he truly saw? For you have believed (πεπίστευκας), O Jew, these things as unlying (ἀψευδέσι) and not only seen by the prophet by a more divine spirit (θειοτέρου πνεύματος) but also spoken and written. To whom is it more worthy to believe, saying that the heavens were opened to him and he heard a voice, or saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting on a throne high and lifted up, Isaiah and Ezekiel or Jesus? For of those no work (ἔργον) so great is found; but the noble deed (ἀνδραγάθημα) of Jesus happened not only at the very times of the embodiment (ἐνσωματώσεως); but even until now the power (δύναμις) of Jesus is working (ἐνεργοῦσα) the conversion (ἐπιστροφή) and improvement (βελτίωσις) in those believing through him in God. And a clear proof (δεῖγμα) that these things happen by his power [is] that, as he himself says and it is perceived (καταλαμβάνεται), there not being workers (ἐργατῶν) working the harvest (θερισμός) of souls, so great is the harvest being gathered (συγκομιζομένων) and brought together into the threshing floors (ἅλωνας) everywhere of God, and churches (ἐκκλησίας).
pass_b_english: First, then, we shall say this. If the man who disbelieves the apparition of the Holy Spirit in the form of the dove had been represented as an Epicurean, or a follower of Democritus, or a Peripatetic, what is said would have fitted the character being portrayed. But as it is, the most wise Celsus has not seen even this: that he has put such an argument in the mouth of a Jew, who believes things from the prophetic Scriptures more numerous and more marvellous than the story of the form of the dove. For someone might say to the Jew, who disbelieves the apparition and thinks he can accuse it as a fiction: And you, sir, how could you prove that the Lord God said to Adam, or to Eve, or to Cain, or to Noah, or to Abraham, or to Isaac, or to Jacob the things that are recorded as said by him to these men (Genesis 2:16; 3:13; 4:6; 6:13; 12:1; 26:2; 28:13)?

And to set one story beside another, I would say to the Jew: Your own Ezekiel too wrote, saying, “The heavens were opened, and I saw a vision of God” (Ezekiel 1:1); and having described it he adds, “This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord; and he said to me” (Ezekiel 1:28; 2:1). For if what is recorded about Jesus is false, since we cannot, as you suppose, clearly show how these things are true, which were seen or heard by him alone and, as you thought you had noticed, by one of those who were punished, why shall we not all the more say that Ezekiel too was telling marvels when he said, “The heavens were opened,” and the rest? Again, when Isaiah says, “I saw the Lord of Hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and the Seraphim stood around him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other” (Isaiah 6:1–2), and the rest, how do you know that he truly saw it? For you, Jew, have believed these things as free of falsehood, and as things that, by a more divine Spirit, were not only seen by the prophet but also spoken and written down.

Who is more worthy of belief when he says that the heavens were opened to him and that he heard a voice, or that he saw “the Lord of Hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1): Isaiah and Ezekiel, or Jesus? For no work of theirs so great is to be found; but the noble work of Jesus did not take place only in the days when he lived in the body. Even to this day the power of Jesus is at work, bringing about conversion and amendment of life in those who believe in God through him. And a clear proof that these things happen by his power is this: though, as he himself says and as one can see, there are no labourers to work at the harvest of souls (Matthew 9:37–38), so great a harvest is being gathered in and brought together into God's threshing floors and churches everywhere.

choices.choice: The Genesis references are representative first instances of God speaking to each person named (Adam 2:16; Eve 3:13; Cain 4:6; Noah 6:13; Abraham 12:1; Isaac 26:2; Jacob 28:13); Origen gives no verses. Ezekiel 1:1 LXX has the plural ὁράσεις θεοῦ; Origen quotes the singular ὅρασιν. The second Ezekiel quotation joins the end of 1:28 (αὕτη ἡ ὅρασις ὁμοιώματος δόξης κυρίου) to the start of 2:1 (καὶ εἶπε πρός με), omitting the intervening words. Isaiah 6:1 LXX has τὸν κύριον without Σαβαώθ; Origen draws Sabaoth from 6:3 or 6:5 (τὸν βασιλέα κύριον σαβαωθ). Sabaoth is rendered 'of Hosts'. The repeated τῷ ἑνί ('to the one... to the one') follows the LXX of 6:2. The sentence εἰ γὰρ ψευδῆ ... κολασθέντων is taken with πῶς as an indirect question governed by παραστῆσαι ('show how these things are true'); the sense 'by him alone' is Jesus, following the Jew's 'except that you say so' in 1.41. Origen's imagined address to the Jew (from 'Your own Ezekiel') is not set in quotation marks, so that double quotation marks stay reserved for Celsus and for Scripture; where the address ends is not marked in the Greek. θειοτέρου πνεύματος is capitalised as the prophetic Spirit, but 'a more divine spirit' in the sense of a higher inspiration is possible. μὴ ὄντων ἐργατῶν: literally 'there being no labourers'; Matthew 9:37 says the labourers are 'few', and the Greek may be compressed or the text short of a word (e.g. πολλῶν); the reading as staged is translated. 'Threshing floors' may also recall Matthew 3:12 (Luke 3:17); not cited inline as uncertain. The staged text has ηντινα without accent; read ἥντινα. Review: ὑπὸ θειοτέρου πνεύματος stands before οὐ μόνον ... ἀλλὰ καί and so governs seen, spoken and written alike; the English now gives it that scope. ἐνσωμάτωσις is rendered 'the days when he lived in the body' (literally 'embodiment') rather than the doctrinal 'incarnation'. εἰς τὰς πανταχοῦ ἅλωνας τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἐκκλησίας: ἐκκλησίας is taken as accusative plural beside ἅλωνας ('God's threshing floors and churches'); the καί may be explanatory ('that is, churches'). The title was changed because Isaiah, unlike Ezekiel, does not say heaven was opened.
